sections.title: 1. Critical Resources & The `counter++` Race Condition
sections.description: How machine-level load/add/store interleaving causes lost updates.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a Lost Update (`counter = counter + 1`)
blocks.content:
A **critical resource** (*ressource critique*) is a non-shareable resource accessed by multiple tasks (e.g., a global variable or a physical peripheral). The code accessing it is a **critical section** (*section critique*), bracketed by an **entry protocol** (*prélude*) and an **exit protocol** (*postlude*).

When two threads each run `counter = counter + 1` $N = 1\,000\,000$ times, the statement compiles to three machine instructions:
```asm
mov counter, r1   ; 1. Load shared counter into private register r1
addi 1, r1        ; 2. Increment local register r1
mov r1, counter   ; 3. Store r1 back to shared counter
```
If a context switch happens after step 1, both threads read the **same** value, increment it locally, and overwrite each other—causing **lost updates**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Classic Exam Question:** With 2 threads each looping $1\,000\,000$ times, what is the **theoretical minimum** final value of `counter`? **Answer: `2`** (not `1,000,000`!).
> *How?* T1 loads `0`, gets preempted. T2 runs $999\,999$ iterations (`counter = 999,999`). T1 resumes and writes `1` (wiping out $999\,999$!). T2 loads `1`, gets preempted. T1 finishes its remaining $999\,999$ iterations, then T2 resumes and writes `2`!

blocks.title: The 4 Rules of a Valid Mutual Exclusion Algorithm
blocks.content:
1. **Mutual Exclusion (*Exclusion mutuelle*):** At any instant, at most **one** task may be in the critical section.
2. **No Deadlock (*Absence d'interblocage / Liveness*):** If tasks are waiting to enter and no task is inside, one waiting task must enter in finite time.
3. **Independence (*Pas de couplage*):** A task's behavior outside the critical section (e.g., crashing/stopping in the non-critical section) must **never** block other tasks.
4. **Symmetry & Fairness (*Pas de famine / Starvation*):** No task plays a privileged role, and no waiting task is starved indefinitely.

sections.title: 2. Why Naive Attempts Fail (Attempts 1–4)
sections.description: Diagnosing each classic failure mode: broken exclusion, strict coupling, and deadlock.

blocks.title: Summary of the 4 Failed Attempts (PCO_3_exclusion.pdf)
blocks.content:
| Attempt | Mechanism | What Goes Wrong? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. `bool occupe`** | `while (occupe); occupe = true;` | **No Mutual Exclusion!** Both threads can see `occupe == false` before either sets `occupe = true`. |
| **2. `int tour`** | `while (tour != 0); ... tour = 1;` | **Strict Alternation / Coupling!** If `T0` stops outside the CS, `T1` is blocked forever waiting for `tour = 1`. |
| **3. `bool etat[2]` (check then set)** | `while (etat[1]); etat[0] = true;` | **No Mutual Exclusion!** Both see `etat[other] == false` and enter simultaneously. |
| **4. `bool etat[2]` (set then check)** | `etat[0] = true; while (etat[1]);` | **Deadlock (*Interblocage*)!** Both set `etat[i] = true` simultaneously, then spin forever waiting for the other. |
| **4b. Set, yield if busy** | Reset `etat[0] = false` inside `while (etat[1])` | **Livelock / Starvation (*Famine*)!** Both can infinitely set, clear, and retry in lockstep. |

sections.title: 3. Dekker's & Peterson's Algorithms + Multi-Core Barriers
sections.description: How Dekker and Peterson achieve software mutual exclusion, and why multi-core CPUs need memory fences.

blocks.title: Peterson's Algorithm (Single-Core vs. Multi-Core)

annotations.note: Politely yield priority to the other thread (tour = 1).
Memory barrier prevents CPU/compiler reordering and forces cache visibility across cores.
Wait ONLY if the other thread wants in AND it is the other thread's turn.

blocks.title: Active Waiting vs. Passive Waiting
blocks.content:
* **Active Waiting (*Attente active*):** The thread wastes CPU cycles spinning in a `while (...) ;` loop testing a condition (e.g., Dekker, Peterson).
* **Passive Waiting (*Attente passive*):** The OS kernel suspends the waiting thread (`bloqué`), freeing the CPU for other ready threads. Requires kernel-supported primitives: **Mutexes**, **Semaphores**, and **Monitors**.

blocks.question: Two threads each increment a shared `static int counter = 0;` `1,000,000` times without synchronization (`counter = counter + 1`). What is the theoretical minimum possible final value of `counter`?
blocks.explanation: Through adversarial context switching between `mov counter, r1` and `mov r1, counter`, T1 can load 0, let T2 run 999,999 times, overwrite counter with 1, let T2 load 1, finish T1's remaining 999,999 iterations, and then T2 writes 2.
hints: Consider what happens if T1 loads `counter = 0` into `r1` and is preempted before writing it back.
Can the same trick be repeated once more on T2's final iteration?

blocks.question: Why do Dekker's and Peterson's algorithms fail on modern multi-core CPUs unless a memory barrier (`std::atomic_thread_fence`) is added?
options: CPU cache coherency delays and out-of-order memory access reordering can allow both threads to read stale values and enter the critical section simultaneously.
C++ `bool` variables are not supported on multi-core processors.
The `tour` variable overflows when two cores access it.
blocks.correct_answer: CPU cache coherency delays and out-of-order memory access reordering can allow both threads to read stale values and enter the critical section simultaneously.
blocks.explanation: Each core has its own store buffer and cache, and compilers/CPUs reorder independent loads and stores. `std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acq_rel)` ensures all prior loads/stores complete and are visible before subsequent loads/stores.
hints: What happens if Core 0 writes `intention[0] = true` to its local store buffer while reading `intention[1]` from cache?
